How we work together

One plan, not eight opinions

Surgeons and physiotherapists in the same room

The surgeons, the sports medicine physician and the physiotherapists meet every Thursday morning to go through the week's complex cases. When a patient needs more than one of us, they see a single written plan rather than a series of separate letters.

Most people see a surgeon first for a diagnosis, then continue with the physiotherapist who will see them most often. If an operation is needed, the surgeon and physiotherapist agree the recovery programme before the day of surgery. If it is not, the same team carries on.

Not sure who to see? Request a visit and tell us where it hurts: our reception team will match you with the right clinician and offer a time that same week.

Okonjo

Orthopedic surgeon, clinical lead

Dr. Amara Okonjo

Knee, sports knee (ACL, meniscus). Clinic days: Mon, Wed, Fri.

Profile

Orthopedic surgeon, clinical lead at Hone Orthopedics

Who you will see and how they work

Amara leads the clinical team at Hone and has focused on the knee for her whole career. Most of her week is spent with people who have hurt a knee playing sport or who have worn one out over decades of work, and she is as comfortable recommending a physiotherapy plan as she is booking an operation.

She sees new knee patients within the same week wherever she can, and she asks every patient to bring their imaging and a list of what they would like to be able to do again. She reviews her own surgical cases with the physiotherapists every month.

pages.title: Conditions & Treatments
pages.content:
Conditions

Knee, shoulder, hip, spine, hand, foot and ankle

What we treat, and how we start

Most joint problems begin with a plan that does not involve an operation. Here is what we see, what we try first and when surgery comes into the conversation.

By joint

Five areas, one directory

Pick the joint that hurts

→KneeLigament, meniscus and arthritis care.→ShoulderCuff, frozen shoulder and instability.→HipPain, impingement and replacement.→SpineNeck and lower back, nerve pain.→Hand, foot & ankleWrist, thumb, heel, bunion and ankle.

Knee

Okonjo · Raman · Talataina

Common conditions

  • ACL and meniscus tears
  • Osteoarthritis
  • Patellofemoral pain
  • Ligament sprains
  • Post-operative recovery

Non-surgical first

Exercise to strengthen the thigh and hip, load advice, a brace if it helps and, where appropriate, an injection. Many meniscus and mild ligament injuries settle without an operation.

When surgery is discussed

Surgery is discussed when a knee locks, gives way despite rehabilitation, or when arthritis limits daily life after the non-surgical options have been tried. Your surgeon explains the options, the usual recovery and the alternatives.

Who treats it

Dr. Amara Okonjo for sports and ligament injuries, Dr. Priya Raman for replacement, and Sina Talataina for rehabilitation.

Shoulder

Brennan · Sorensen

Common conditions

  • Rotator cuff tears and tendinopathy
  • Frozen shoulder
  • Instability and dislocation
  • Acromioclavicular sprains
  • Elbow tendon pain

Non-surgical first

Graded exercise, activity changes and sometimes an injection. Most cuff and frozen-shoulder problems improve with a structured programme over weeks to months.

When surgery is discussed

Surgery is considered for a significant tear in an active person, for repeated dislocations and for problems that have not improved with a proper course of rehabilitation.

Who treats it

Dr. Lucas Brennan assesses the shoulder and elbow; Mikkel Sorensen writes the post-operative programme.

Hip

Raman · Sorensen

Common conditions

  • Hip osteoarthritis
  • Femoroacetabular impingement
  • Bursitis and tendon pain
  • Pain after a fall
  • Hip replacement and recovery

Non-surgical first

Walking programmes, strength work, a stick, weight management advice and pain-relief options. Many people manage hip arthritis for years without surgery.

When surgery is discussed

A replacement is discussed when pain disturbs sleep, limits walking or independence and the non-surgical options are no longer enough. Dr. Raman explains the operation, the risks and the first six weeks.

Who treats it

Dr. Priya Raman for surgery and Mikkel Sorensen for rehabilitation.

Spine

Ferreira · Sorensen

Common conditions

  • Lower back pain
  • Sciatica and disc problems
  • Neck pain and arm symptoms
  • Spinal stenosis
  • Post-operative spine rehab

Non-surgical first

Staying active, a movement programme, short-term pain relief and reassurance. Most back pain improves over weeks; scans are used only when they will change the plan.

When surgery is discussed

Surgery is discussed for nerve symptoms that are getting worse or have not settled over a suitable period, and for specific structural problems found on a scan.

Who treats it

Dr. Tomás Ferreira for assessment and surgery, Mikkel Sorensen for spine rehabilitation.

Hand, foot & ankle

Cho · Whitfield

Common conditions

  • Carpal tunnel and trigger finger
  • Thumb and wrist arthritis
  • Heel pain and bunions
  • Recurring ankle sprains
  • Foot and ankle tendon pain

Non-surgical first

Splints, exercises, footwear changes, injections and a therapist-led programme. Many hand and foot problems improve without an operation.

When surgery is discussed

Surgery is considered when numbness is persistent, a joint is painful or unstable despite treatment, or a deformity limits shoes and activity. Most hand and foot operations are day cases.

Who treats it

Dr. Helen Cho for hands, wrists, feet and ankles, with Dr. Grace Whitfield for sports-related ankle problems.

Booking

Request by Wednesday 17:00

Not sure which joint to start with?

Describe where it hurts when you request a visit and our reception team will match you with the clinician who sees that joint most often. We reply within one business day, by 18:00, and you are seen the same week.

A consultation with a surgeon is $240 (40 minutes). Follow-up consultations are $140. See Fees & Insurance for every price.

pages.title: Sports Injury
pages.content:
Sports Injury

Physician and physiotherapist together, in one visit

From the twist or the tweak to back on the field

Whether the injury was sudden or built up over a season, the sports injury assessment gives you a diagnosis, a plan and a sensible next step the same week.

Three starting points

Acute, overuse, return-to-play

Where are you in the injury?

→Acute injuryA sprain, tear or fall: what to do in the first 48 hours and when to be seen.→Overuse injuryPain that builds with training: tendons, shins, hips and backs.→Return-to-play testingStrength, balance and running checks before full training.

Acute injury

Sprains, strains, tears

First 48 hours

Protect the joint, keep it moving within comfort, and note whether you can put weight on it. Swelling that increases, a joint that gives way, numbness or pain at night are reasons to book promptly.

What we do

The sports injury assessment is 50 minutes with Dr. Grace Whitfield and a physiotherapist in the room. We examine the joint, scan on site if it helps (ultrasound $160, X-ray $85) and write a plan before you leave.

Overuse injury

Tendons, shins, stress injuries

Why it builds

Overuse injuries usually follow a change in training: more distance, a new surface, new shoes or too little recovery. The pain is often mild at first and easy to ignore.

What we do

We look at load, technique and strength together, and usually keep you training in a modified way. Imaging is used only when the examination suggests it will change the plan.

Return-to-play testing

Before full training

The tests

Return-to-play testing includes hop and single-leg strength tests, balance work and a graded running check with the physiotherapist. It tells you where you are, not when you will be fully recovered.

Working with coaches

With your permission we write a short summary for your coach or trainer, covering what you can do now, what to avoid and what comes next. We do not promise outcomes or timelines; recovery differs from person to person.

Sports injury assessment

$195 · 50 minutes

One visit, two clinicians

The assessment costs $195 and takes 50 minutes. It is held with a sports medicine physician and a physiotherapist together, so that the diagnosis and the first week of the plan arrive at the same time. Follow-up physiotherapy sessions are $110 (45 minutes), or $600 for a pack of six.

Request by Wednesday 17:00 and we reply within one business day with a time the same week.

Book the assessment

Bring any imaging, your usual training shoes and a note of what you are training for.

Call (604) 555-0142Request a visit

pages.title: Physiotherapy & Rehabilitation
pages.content:
Physiotherapy

Programmes written for your joint

Rehab you can practise on our floor and at home

Two physiotherapists, a rehab floor with plinths, bars and bands, and a written plan you can follow at home.

Programmes

Three kinds of plan

Where most rehabilitation starts

→Post-operative programmesWritten before surgery, adjusted at each visit, shared with your surgeon.→Sport and running rehabStrength, load and return-to-run progressions for active people.→Balance and ankle workFor sprains, instability and general confidence on your feet.

Post-operative programmes

Shoulder, hip, knee, spine

How it works

Mikkel Sorensen writes your programme before the day of surgery. You meet on the rehab floor, practise the first exercises and receive a printed plan that you take home.

Visits

Most people attend once or twice a week at the start, then less often as they progress. Each visit is 45 minutes and costs $110.

Sport and running rehab

Return-to-run and field sports

Graded return

Sina Talataina builds a progression of strength, hopping and running tests so that you can see your own progress. We never promise a return date; recovery differs from person to person.

Home exercise plans

Every plan comes with photographs of the exercises on our own rehab floor and a note of how many to do and how often. You can request changes at any visit.

Balance and ankle work

Sprains and instability

What it covers

Single-leg balance, a wobble board, calf and hip strength, and gradual return to jumping and cutting for those who need it.

Who it is for

Teenagers after repeated sprains, older adults who want to feel steadier and anyone who has had an ankle that keeps giving way.

Prices

Physiotherapy in plain figures

A single session or a pack of six

A single physiotherapy session (45 minutes) is $110. A pack of six sessions is $600, which is $100 a session. Packs are used within a year and can be shared across joints if you are recovering from more than one injury.

We issue itemised receipts that you can send to your extended health plan.

pages.title: Your First Visit
pages.content:
First visit

Request by Wednesday 17:00, be seen this week

What to expect when you arrive

A first visit takes 60 to 75 minutes. Here is how to request it, what to bring and what happens on the day.

Before you come

Four small things

What to bring

Request a visit online or call (604) 555-0142 by Wednesday 17:00. We reply within one business day, by 18:00, with a time. Your first visit is the same week, Monday to Saturday.

  • Any imaging you have (X-ray, MRI, ultrasound), on a disc or a link
  • A list of your medications and allergies
  • A referral letter if you have one (optional; we see self-referred patients)
  • Shorts or loose clothing if it is a lower-limb problem

We can take X-rays on site (2 views, $85) and perform a diagnostic ultrasound of one joint ($160) during the same visit if the clinician thinks it will help.

On the day

60 to 75 minutes

What happens at the visit

You are greeted at reception, shown to a consultation room and seen by the clinician you were matched with. They ask what has happened, what you want to get back to, examine the joint and talk through the next step. Imaging, if needed, is done on site.

Before you leave you receive a plan in writing, a date for a follow-up if you need one and a clear list of what to do in the meantime. If a surgeon recommends physiotherapy first, we can book the first session before you go.

A new patient consultation with a surgeon is $240 (40 minutes of consulting time within the 60 to 75 minute visit). Cancellation with less than 24 hours' notice is $50.

pages.title: Patient Stories
pages.content:
Stories

Four people, four joints

What recovery looked like for them

Real recovery has different speeds. These four short stories are individual experiences, not predictions.

Stories

Knee, shoulder, hip, ankle

Four patients, in their words

→Maya, 34trail runner · KneeMaya tore her meniscus on a descent and came in for a sports injury assessment the same week.→Daniel, 58carpenter · ShoulderDaniel could no longer lift a sheet of plywood.→Rosa, 71retired teacher · HipRosa had stopped walking her dog because of hip pain.→Kenji, 19basketball player · AnkleKenji had sprained the same ankle four times.

Maya, 34, trail runner

Knee

Maya tore her meniscus on a descent and came in for a sports injury assessment the same week. With Sina she worked through eight weeks of physiotherapy, and was back to short trail runs at week ten.

Individual experience. Recovery differs from person to person; your clinician will talk through what to expect for you.

Daniel, 58, carpenter

Shoulder

Daniel could no longer lift a sheet of plywood. An ultrasound showed a rotator cuff tear; Dr. Brennan repaired it, Mikkel wrote his post-operative programme, and four months later he was back at the bench part-time.

Individual experience. Recovery differs from person to person; your clinician will talk through what to expect for you.

Rosa, 71, retired teacher

Hip

Rosa had stopped walking her dog because of hip pain. After a hip replacement with Dr. Raman she was walking round the block at six weeks.

Individual experience. Recovery differs from person to person; your clinician will talk through what to expect for you.

Kenji, 19, basketball player

Ankle

Kenji had sprained the same ankle four times. Dr. Whitfield and Sina built a balance programme, and he finished the season with no further sprains.

Individual experience. Recovery differs from person to person; your clinician will talk through what to expect for you.

pages.title: About the Clinic
pages.content:
About

Founded in 2011 on Main Street

An orthopedic and sports injury clinic in Mount Pleasant

Hone began with two surgeons and one physiotherapist in a single room. Today eight clinicians share one building at 2180 Main Street, Vancouver.

Our story

Since 2011

Surgeons and physiotherapists under one roof

Hone Orthopedics opened in 2011 with a simple idea: people with joint problems should see the clinician who specialises in that joint, and the physiotherapist who will help them recover should be down the corridor rather than across the city.

Over the years the team grew to five orthopedic surgeons, one sports medicine physician and two physiotherapists: eight clinicians in total. Each of them has a clinic day on the specialist directory, and each case is reviewed together on Thursday mornings.

The clinic is in Mount Pleasant, Vancouver, with a step-free entrance, street parking and a bus stop at the door. We are open Monday to Friday 7:30–19:00 and Saturday 8:00–13:00.

How we work

Three habits

What stays the same

Non-surgical first. For most conditions, exercise, load advice and time come first. Surgery is discussed when it is the right answer, not before.

Same week. Request by Wednesday 17:00, hear from us within one business day and be seen the same week.

posts.title: How to tell a sprain from something more
posts.content:
Most sprained ankles and wrists settle in a couple of weeks with sensible care. A few are something more: a fracture, a torn ligament or a tendon injury. The first 48 hours give you most of the clues.

Questions to ask yourself

Can you put weight on it and take four steps? Did you hear or feel a crack at the time? Is there bruising that spreads, numbness, or pain over the bone itself rather than the soft tissue? Any of these is a reason to be seen sooner.

What helps in the first two days

Keep the joint moving within comfort, support it if it feels unstable and elevate it when resting. Avoid long walks on a swollen ankle. If swelling is increasing at 48 hours or you still cannot walk normally, book a sports injury assessment ($195, 50 minutes), where we can scan on site if needed.

This article is general information, not a diagnosis. If something is worrying you, request a visit or call (604) 555-0142.

posts.title: Step-ups: the exercise behind most knee plans
posts.excerpt: Why we start with a box of the right height.
posts.content:
If you have ever had a knee plan from a physiotherapist, there is a good chance it included a step-up. It is simple, needs almost no equipment and trains the thigh, hip and balance together.

Choosing the box

Start with a step that is low enough to climb without pain, usually 10 to 15 centimetres. Stand tall, step up with one leg, lower slowly and keep the knee in line with the second toe.

How many

Most people begin with two sets of eight to ten on each side, a few times a week, and add height or a light weight when it feels easy. Your physiotherapist will adjust this for your own knee.

If the exercise causes sharp pain, stop and ask. Sina or Mikkel can show you the right height on our rehab floor in a single 45 minute session ($110).

This article is general information, not a diagnosis. If something is worrying you, request a visit or call (604) 555-0142.

posts.title: What to bring to your first rehab session
posts.excerpt: Clothing, shoes, and the questions worth asking.
posts.content:
A first physiotherapy session is mostly a conversation and an assessment, followed by a few exercises. A little preparation makes it more useful.

What to wear

Loose clothing you can move in, and shorts for a lower-limb problem or a tank top for a shoulder. Bring the shoes you walk or train in, not your best pair.

What to bring

Any imaging or surgical notes, a list of your medications and your goal in one sentence: for example, "walk the dog for 30 minutes" or "return to a weekly 5 km run".

Questions worth asking

How often should I come? What should I do at home every day? What should make me call you sooner? Each session is 45 minutes ($110), or buy a pack of six for $600.

This article is general information, not a diagnosis. If something is worrying you, request a visit or call (604) 555-0142.

posts.title: What happens at a shoulder ultrasound
posts.excerpt: A short look at the scan we can do the same visit.
posts.content:
A diagnostic ultrasound uses sound waves, not radiation, to look at the tendons and bursa of one joint. At Hone it costs $160 and is done on site during your visit when the clinician thinks it will help.

What you will do

You sit or lie comfortably while a gel is applied and a small probe moves over the shoulder. The clinician may ask you to lift or rotate the arm so they can see the tendons move.

What it can show

It can show a rotator cuff tear, a thickened tendon, fluid in the bursa or calcium deposits. It cannot see everything: sometimes an X-ray ($85, 2 views) or an MRI is the better test.

You will leave with the findings explained, and a plan that fits them.

This article is general information, not a diagnosis. If something is worrying you, request a visit or call (604) 555-0142.

posts.title: Returning to running after a knee injury
posts.content:
Many runners ask how many weeks it will be before they can run again after a knee injury. A calendar is a poor guide: some people are ready in weeks and others take months. Testing is a better one.

The usual steps

First walking without a limp, then strength on a single leg, then hopping and short jogging intervals on a flat surface. Each stage is checked by a physiotherapist before the next.

Warning signs

Pain that gets worse during a session, swelling the next morning or a sense that the knee gives way are reasons to pause and ask. We do not promise timelines; recovery differs from person to person.

Sina Talataina runs return-to-run programmes on Monday to Friday; the sports injury assessment ($195) is a good place to start.

This article is general information, not a diagnosis. If something is worrying you, request a visit or call (604) 555-0142.

posts.title: Preparing for a joint replacement
posts.excerpt: What the weeks before surgery are for.
posts.content:
If you and your surgeon have decided on a hip or knee replacement, the weeks before the operation matter more than most people think. Strength, home set-up and a clear plan make the first weeks easier.

Before the day

Practise the exercises you will do after surgery, so that they are familiar. Set up a chair of the right height, clear loose rugs and plan who will help in the first week.

What we do at Hone

Dr. Raman explains the operation and recovery in the consultation ($240, 40 minutes), and the physiotherapist writes the programme before the day of surgery so that you meet the person who will see you afterwards.

Recovery differs from person to person, and your surgeon will explain what to expect for you.

This article is general information, not a diagnosis. If something is worrying you, request a visit or call (604) 555-0142.
